    Ambient RNA removal with CellSweep¶

    Python port of the R vignette Ambient RNA removal with CellSweep. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

    Intro¶

    Cells lyse during dissociation and their transcripts end up in the buffer. Every droplet then gets loaded with a bit of that soup on top of whatever cell it caught, which is why you find monocyte genes in T cells, haemoglobin everywhere, and lineage markers that refuse to be clean. That background is the ambient RNA.

    CellSweep attacks it as a mixture problem. Every observed count in a barcode comes from one of three places: the ambient profile of that emulsion, a global bulk profile, or the barcode's own cell type profile. An EM fit splits the counts three ways per barcode, and subtracting the first two components leaves the denoised matrix. The per-barcode ambient fraction, alpha, falls out of the same fit, which doubles as a quality metric: a barcode that is 60% soup is not a cell you want in your clustering.

    Two things about where this sits in a workflow, because both are easy to get wrong.

    It runs after annotation, not before. The model subtracts against cell type profiles, so it needs the labels on input. The chain is: ingest the raw barcodes, cluster and annotate as usual, then bv.doublets.cellsweep(), then redo the feature selection and reduction on the clean counts.

    It needs the empty droplets. The ambient profile is estimated from their pooled counts, and they stay in the EM with their contamination fraction pinned at 1. So the object has to be ingested permissively. The load-time cutoffs in bixverse are irreversible, and the defaults delete exactly the barcodes the model trains on.

    The raw matrix¶

    We use the 10x Genomics 5' PBMC 1k run, the same data the CellSweep reference notebook works through. This is the unfiltered matrix, so every barcode the sequencer saw is in there.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    h5_path = bv.io.download_pbmc_1k_5p()

meta = bv.io.read_tenx_h5_metadata(h5_path)
print(meta["dims"])
meta["feature_types"]
    h5_path = bv.io.download_pbmc_1k_5p() meta = bv.io.read_tenx_h5_metadata(h5_path) print(meta["dims"]) meta["feature_types"]

    Out[2]:
    {'Antibody Capture': 19, 'Gene Expression': 36601}

    737,280 barcodes and 36,620 features, of which 19 are Antibody Capture. Only the gene expression ones are wanted here, which is what feature_type selects.

    Now the permissive load. min_lib_size=1 throws away the barcodes that saw no molecule at all, which is most of them, and keeps everything else.

    h5_path,
    qc=MinQualityParams(min_unique_genes=0, min_lib_size=1, min_cells=0),
    feature_type="Gene Expression",
    verbose=True,
)

    98k barcodes carrying at least one UMI. The vast majority are empty droplets and that is the point: they are the training data for the soup.

    Calling the empty droplets¶

    EmptyDropletsParams offers four ways to decide which barcode is empty, in descending order of how much you should trust them. "supplied" takes an existing boolean column from the obs table, and if you have Cell Ranger's filtered barcode list you already know the answer. The other three infer it from the library sizes alone.

    The barcode rank curve is the thing they are all trying to read.

ax.set_yscale("log")

    The cliff is obvious. Roughly a thousand barcodes sit well above it and everything else falls off to single-digit libraries.

    bv.doublets.infer_empty_droplets() is the Rust side of the three inference methods, exposed so the calls can be compared before committing to one.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    methods = {
    "umi_cutoff": EmptyDropletsParams(method="umi_cutoff", umi_cutoff=257),
    "expected_cells": EmptyDropletsParams(method="expected_cells", expected_cells=1000),
    "knee": EmptyDropletsParams(method="knee"),
}

lib_size = obs_raw["lib_size"].to_numpy()

rows = []
for name, params in methods.items():
    call = bv.doublets.infer_empty_droplets(lib_size, params)
    rows.append(
        {
            "method": name,
            "empty": int(call.sum()),
            "kept": int((~call).sum()),
            "min_kept_lib_size": int(lib_size[~call].min()),
        }
    )

comparison = pl.DataFrame(rows)

comparison

    umi_cutoff and expected_cells land on the same thousand barcodes, which they should: the cutoff the notebook quotes is the one you get by asking for a thousand cells. The knee detector stops at 120 UMIs instead of 257 and hands back 19 extra barcodes. It is experimental in the reference too, so treat it as a starting point rather than an answer.

    Annotating the real cells¶

    CellSweep needs cell type labels, so the real barcodes have to go through a normal pipeline first. The raw object is not the place to do that, since 97k of its barcodes are soup. Load the same file a second time with QC that means something, and cluster there.

    qc=MinQualityParams(min_unique_genes=200, min_lib_size=257, min_cells=3),
    feature_type="Gene Expression",
    verbose=True,
)

    Good enough to subtract against; you would name them with bv.annotate.calc_sc_type_scores() or a reference in a real analysis, but the model only cares that barcodes with the same label share a profile.

    Putting the labels back¶

    The labels live on the cell object and CellSweep reads them off the raw one, so they have to be joined across by barcode. Every barcode that is not a clustered cell keeps a null, which is exactly how cellsweep() finds the barcodes it should ignore.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    labels = obs_raw.select("cell_idx", "cell_id").join(
    obs_cells.select(
        "cell_id",
        pl.format("cluster_{}", pl.col("leiden_clusters")).alias("cell_type"),
    ),
    on="cell_id",
    how="left",
)

raw_object.add_obs(
    labels.select("cell_idx", "cell_type").with_columns(sample_id=pl.lit("pbmc_1k"))
)

labels["cell_type"].value_counts().sort("cell_type")
    labels = obs_raw.select("cell_idx", "cell_id").join( obs_cells.select( "cell_id", pl.format("cluster_{}", pl.col("leiden_clusters")).alias("cell_type"), ), on="cell_id", how="left", ) raw_object.add_obs( labels.select("cell_idx", "cell_type").with_columns(sample_id=pl.lit("pbmc_1k")) ) labels["cell_type"].value_counts().sort("cell_type")

    Watch the null handling there. Formatting the label before the join keeps the unmatched barcodes null. Paste a prefix onto the joined column the wrong way and you get the string "cluster_null", and CellSweep will happily treat those barcodes as one more cell type and fit a profile to them. Keep the null a null.

    sample_id is a constant here because this is one emulsion. It is still required: the ambient profile is a property of a single run, and pooling samples into one profile is wrong even when it runs.

    Three numbers in that output are worth reading. 96,998 barcodes went into the ambient profile. 845 got denoised. And 155 barcodes were neither: they cleared the UMI cutoff but failed QC or the outlier check, so they have no label to subtract against. Those are dropped from the fit and from the output, which is why the clean object is 845 cells and not 1000.

    The denoised counts land in a new directory. The raw layer takes stochastically rounded values so the negative binomial methods downstream still see integers, and the normalised layer keeps the float magnitudes.

    What came out¶

    The ambient profile is the first thing to look at, because it is the one part of the fit you can sanity check against what you know about the tissue.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    var_clean = clean_object.var()

top_ambient = var_clean.sort("cellsweep_ambient", descending=True).head(20)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5), layout="constrained")
ax.barh(
    top_ambient["gene_name"].to_list()[::-1],
    top_ambient["cellsweep_ambient"].to_numpy()[::-1],
    color=colours[1],
)
ax.set_xlabel("Fraction of the ambient profile")

plt.show()
    var_clean = clean_object.var() top_ambient = var_clean.sort("cellsweep_ambient", descending=True).head(20) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5), layout="constrained") ax.barh( top_ambient["gene_name"].to_list()[::-1], top_ambient["cellsweep_ambient"].to_numpy()[::-1], color=colours[1], ) ax.set_xlabel("Fraction of the ambient profile") ax.set_title("What the soup is made of") plt.show()

    MALAT1, elongation factors, ribosomal proteins, B2M, mitochondrial genes. That is the soup of a lysing PBMC and nothing else, which is a good sign.

    This run is clean. The median barcode is essentially uncontaminated and only a handful sit above the 0.3 the reference notebook filters at. That is not always what you get, and it is worth knowing before you assume your lineage markers are real.

    Does the subtraction do anything?¶

    The honest test is not whether alpha looks plausible but whether the counts change in the direction they should. Monocyte genes appearing in T cells are soup by construction, so track a couple of them across clusters, before and after.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    markers = {"LYZ": "monocyte", "S100A8": "monocyte", "PPBP": "platelet"}
marker_ids = dict(
    var_clean.filter(pl.col("gene_name").is_in(list(markers)))
    .select("gene_id", "gene_name")
    .iter_rows()
)


def detection_rate(object, layer_name):
    expr = bv.pl.extract_gene_expression(
        object, list(marker_ids), obs_cols=["cell_type"]
    ).filter(pl.col("cell_type").is_not_null())
    return (
        expr.unpivot(
            index=["cell_id", "cell_type"], variable_name="gene_id", value_name="expr"
        )
        .with_columns(gene=pl.col("gene_id").replace_strict(marker_ids))
        .group_by("gene", "cell_type")
        .agg(detected=(pl.col("expr") > 0).mean())
        .with_columns(layer=pl.lit(layer_name))
    )


rates = pl.concat(
    [detection_rate(raw_object, "raw"), detection_rate(clean_object, "denoised")]
)

with pl.Config(tbl_rows=-1):

        rates.pivot("layer", index=["gene", "cell_type"], values="detected").sort(
            "gene", "cell_type"
        )
    )

    Cluster 1 is the monocytes and it keeps LYZ and S100A8 in essentially every cell. The small myeloid cluster 8 keeps exactly the rates it came in with, 92% for LYZ and 69% for S100A8. Everywhere else those genes were showing up in a few percent of barcodes before the sweep and are gone afterwards. PPBP does the same thing in reverse: platelet transcripts leaking into the monocytes roughly halve. The subtraction went after the right counts.

    Reprocessing the clean counts¶

    Feature selection and reduction were computed on contaminated counts, so they have to be redone. Drop the barcodes CellSweep says are mostly soup while you are at it.

)

bv.pp.calculate_pca(clean_object, no_pcs=30, sparse_svd=True)

bv.graph.find_neighbours(
    clean_object, neighbours_params=NeighboursParams(knn_method="exhaustive")
)

bv.embed.umap(clean_object)

    The clusters survive the sweep, which is what you want. CellSweep is not supposed to rearrange your populations, it is supposed to stop the space between them being filled with borrowed transcripts. If your structure falls apart after denoising, the labels you handed it were wrong.

    Where this goes next¶

    The obvious extension is multi-sample data, where the ambient profile is fitted per emulsion and sample_column starts earning its keep. A soup that differs between runs is a batch effect that no correction method will name for you, and having cellsweep_alpha and the per-sample profiles in hand is a much better starting point than pretending the contamination is uniform.

    cellsweep_alpha is also worth keeping in the obs table after the fact. It is a QC metric in its own right, and a cluster with a suspiciously high median is usually debris rather than biology.
